results.name: set_level_yes_rate_sd
results.description: Standard deviation across sets (with >=3 distinct targets) of each set's mean yes-rate; observed > null means overall willingness to say yes varies between sets more than the model's single bias/slope mapping from summed similarity produces (set-specific rule breadth), observed < null means less.
results.code:
# name: set_level_yes_rate_sd
# description: Standard deviation across sets (with >=3 distinct targets) of each set's mean yes-rate; observed > null means overall willingness to say yes varies between sets more than the model's single bias/slope mapping from summed similarity produces (set-specific rule breadth), observed < null means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    g = df.groupby("number_set").agg(m=("rating", "mean"), k=("target", "nunique"))
    g = g[g["k"] >= 3]
    return float(g["m"].std()) if len(g) > 1 else 0.0

results.name: common_divisor_nodigit_contrast
results.description: In multi-example sets whose examples' greatest common divisor is >=3, among targets sharing no example's final digit, yes-rate for targets divisible by that gcd minus for non-divisible targets; observed > null means people infer an arithmetic 'multiples of g' rule more strongly than the model's per-example coprimality penalty captures, observed < null means less.
results.code:
# name: common_divisor_nodigit_contrast
# description: In multi-example sets whose examples' greatest common divisor is >=3, among targets sharing no example's final digit, yes-rate for targets divisible by that gcd minus for non-divisible targets; observed > null means people infer an arithmetic 'multiples of g' rule more strongly than the model's per-example coprimality penalty captures, observed < null means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(1)
    exi = np.where(np.isnan(ex), 0, ex).astype(int)
    g = np.gcd.reduce(exi, axis=1)
    dig = np.mod(ex, 10)
    anydig = np.nansum((dig == np.mod(t, 10)[:, None]).astype(float), 1) > 0
    base = (n >= 2) & (g >= 3) & ~anydig
    div = np.mod(t, np.maximum(g, 1)) == 0
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    a = base & div; b = base & ~div
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: far_digit_match_rate
results.description: In sets of >=2 examples that all share one final digit, the yes-rate for targets that share that digit but lie >=15 from every example; observed > null means people apply the final-digit (e.g. multiples-of-10) rule beyond magnitude neighbourhood more than the model's distance-decaying similarity allows, observed < null means they generalize the digit less far.
results.code:
# name: far_digit_match_rate
# description: In sets of >=2 examples that all share one final digit, the yes-rate for targets that share that digit but lie >=15 from every example; observed > null means people apply the final-digit (e.g. multiples-of-10) rule beyond magnitude neighbourhood more than the model's distance-decaying similarity allows, observed < null means they generalize the digit less far.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(1)
    dig = np.where(np.isnan(ex), np.nan, np.mod(ex, 10))
    same = (np.nanmax(dig, 1) == np.nanmin(dig, 1)) & (n >= 2)
    tmatch = np.mod(t, 10) == np.nanmin(dig, 1)
    dmin = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), 1)
    m = same & tmatch & (dmin >= 15)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy()
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() else 0.0

results.name: exact_example_target_rate
results.description: Yes-rate on trials whose target is identical to one of the set's examples; observed < null means people endorse the shown examples themselves less often than the model's maximal self-similarity predicts (i.e. a ceiling / response-noise floor the model lacks), observed > null means more.
results.code:
# name: exact_example_target_rate
# description: Yes-rate on trials whose target is identical to one of the set's examples; observed < null means people endorse the shown examples themselves less often than the model's maximal self-similarity predicts (i.e. a ceiling / response-noise floor the model lacks), observed > null means more.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    m = (ex == t[:, None]).any(1)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy()
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() else 0.0

results.name: trial_index_drift_corr
results.description: Correlation between trial_index and the yes response across all trials; observed above/below null means people's yes-rate drifts up/down over the session, which the stationary model cannot produce.

results.name: digit_homog_near_nomatch_rate
results.description: In sets of >=2 examples all sharing one final digit, the yes-rate for targets within 10 of some example that do NOT share that digit; observed < null means people reject magnitude-near digit violators more strictly than the model's coincidence-sharpened similarity predicts, observed > null means magnitude still wins more than predicted.
results.code:
# name: digit_homog_near_nomatch_rate
# description: In sets of >=2 examples all sharing one final digit, the yes-rate for targets within 10 of some example that do NOT share that digit; observed < null means people reject magnitude-near digit violators more strictly than the model's coincidence-sharpened similarity predicts, observed > null means magnitude still wins more than predicted.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(1)
    dig = np.mod(ex, 10)
    same = (np.nanmax(dig, 1) == np.nanmin(dig, 1)) & (n >= 2)
    tmatch = np.mod(t, 10) == np.nanmin(dig, 1)
    dmin = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), 1)
    m = same & ~tmatch & (dmin <= 10)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy()
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() else 0.0

results.name: parity_set_distance_corr
results.description: In sets of >=3 examples all of one parity but not all one final digit, among parity-matching targets that share no example's final digit, the correlation of yes with distance to the nearest example; observed closer to 0 (or above null) means people treat such sets as a parity rule with flat endorsement, while the model's magnitude similarity predicts a more negative distance gradient.
results.code:
# name: parity_set_distance_corr
# description: In sets of >=3 examples all of one parity but not all one final digit, among parity-matching targets that share no example's final digit, the correlation of yes with distance to the nearest example; observed closer to 0 (or above null) means people treat such sets as a parity rule with flat endorsement, while the model's magnitude similarity predicts a more negative distance gradient.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(1)
    par = np.mod(ex, 2); dig = np.mod(ex, 10)
    samepar = (np.nanmax(par, 1) == np.nanmin(par, 1)) & (n >= 3)
    samedig = np.nanmax(dig, 1) == np.nanmin(dig, 1)
    tpar = np.mod(t, 2) == np.nanmin(par, 1)
    anydig = np.nansum((dig == np.mod(t, 10)[:, None]).astype(float), 1) > 0
    dmin = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), 1)
    m = samepar & ~samedig & tpar & ~anydig
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)[m]; d = dmin[m]
    if m.sum() < 3 or r.std() == 0 or d.std() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.corrcoef(r, d)[0, 1])

results.name: same_decade_near_contrast
results.description: Among targets 1-5 away from their nearest example and sharing no example's final digit, yes-rate when the target is in the same decade (same tens digit) as that nearest example minus when it is in a different decade; observed > null means people use a decade/tens-digit category the model lacks, observed < null means decade boundaries matter less than distance-matched similarity predicts.
results.code:
# name: same_decade_near_contrast
# description: Among targets 1-5 away from their nearest example and sharing no example's final digit, yes-rate when the target is in the same decade (same tens digit) as that nearest example minus when it is in a different decade; observed > null means people use a decade/tens-digit category the model lacks, observed < null means decade boundaries matter less than distance-matched similarity predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    dig = np.mod(ex, 10)
    d = np.abs(ex - t[:, None])
    d = np.where(np.isnan(d), 1e9, d)
    idx = d.argmin(1)
    near = ex[np.arange(len(t)), idx]
    dmin = d[np.arange(len(t)), idx]
    anydig = np.nansum((dig == np.mod(t, 10)[:, None]).astype(float), 1) > 0
    dec_t = np.minimum(t, 99) // 10; dec_e = np.minimum(near, 99) // 10
    m = (dmin >= 1) & (dmin <= 5) & ~anydig
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    a = m & (dec_t == dec_e); b = m & (dec_t != dec_e)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
